chunks: "A sensor is a device that converts some physical quantity, like temperature, light, acceleration or pressure, into an electrical signal that a circuit can read.

The part that actually reacts to the physics is the sensing element: a thermistor's resistance changes with temperature, a photodiode makes current from photons, a MEMS accelerometer's capacitance changes when a tiny mass moves.
But a sensor on its own is rarely useful, so I think of it as a chain. The sensing element makes a small, often nonlinear, analog signal.
Signal conditioning cleans that up: a voltage divider or bridge to turn resistance into voltage, an amplifier for gain, a filter to remove noise.
An ADC turns it into a number, and firmware applies calibration and converts it to engineering units. Many modern sensors package all of that and just give you I2C or SPI.
When I choose one, I look at range, sensitivity, resolution, accuracy, noise, bandwidth and drift.

For example a 10 kilohms NTC thermistor is very sensitive, about minus 4 percent per kelvin near room temperature, but it is nonlinear and only so accurate, whereas a thermocouple is rugged and wide range but only tens of microvolts per degree.
Which one is right depends entirely on the application."
